lesson.title: Routing at Home: How Traffic Moves Inside One Network
lesson.summary: Intradomain routing is routing within a single autonomous system, where cooperative, administratively unified routers, such as those running RIP or OSPF, can safely chase a single shared cost metric.
lesson.body:
With autonomous systems established as the basic unit of the internet, it becomes useful to give a name to the two very different routing problems that exist inside versus between those units. Intradomain routing, also called interior gateway routing, is routing within a single autonomous system, among routers that all belong to one administratively unified network and can be assumed to cooperate honestly and completely.

This is the setting where both RIP and OSPF operate, RIP as a simple distance vector protocol and OSPF as the link state protocol covered earlier, and it is worth noticing what they have in common despite being built on opposite routing algorithms. Both assume every router within the domain is under common control, both are configured to optimize a single, network wide notion of cost, hop count for RIP, typically bandwidth derived cost for OSPF, and neither has any concept of business policy, because inside one organization there is no business relationship to encode, just an engineering goal of moving traffic efficiently and reliably between routers the operator controls. That shared assumption is exactly what makes it safe for OSPF to flood full topology information to every router in the domain, and it is why intradomain protocols can afford to chase a literal shortest or lowest cost path without worrying about whether that path crosses a partner's network or a competitor's.

Intradomain routing's job, concretely, is to get a packet from wherever it enters an AS to the correct exit point, the border router that has the best route out toward the packet's actual destination, which very often lies outside the AS entirely. That handoff, from getting a packet to the right edge of a network to getting it the rest of the way across the internet, is precisely the boundary where intradomain routing stops and interdomain routing takes over, and it is why real networks typically run an interior protocol like OSPF internally at the same time as they run BGP at their borders, each protocol solving the piece of the problem it was actually designed for.
